From restraint to relationship.

Thom Sullivan speaks with David Brimfield about what happens when training is treated not as a set of physical skills, but as a long-term risk-reduction framework built around confidence, evidence and human rights.

See the participant outcomeExplore the learning
David BrimfieldUnique Support Services
Thom SullivanMaybo, New Zealand
A remarkable outcome

Freedom increased. Restrictions reduced.

One young participant arrived with a high level of risk and 17 restrictive practices in place. Over several years, careful review, stronger reporting and a prevention-led approach helped reduce that number to seven.

17

Restrictive practices at the outset

Including four physical interventions and several routine environmental restrictions.

7

Restrictive practices in the updated plan

The result of sustained evidence gathering, review and collaboration rather than a quick fix.

99%

Access at baseline

The participant could use their kitchen, cook and enjoy their own home for the great majority of the time.

The risk-reduction model

Start with “why?”, not “how long?”

The conversation repeatedly returns to one principle: before asking how to hold someone, ask why any physical intervention is being considered at all.

1

Understand the person

Look beyond the immediate behaviour to sleep, relationships, life events, communication and the person’s wider journey.

2

Strengthen primary responses

Build staff confidence in prevention, withdrawal, observation, de-escalation and dynamic risk assessment.

3

Capture better evidence

Record what led up to the incident, what happened and which strategies did or did not work.

4

Return freedom safely

Use evidence to challenge routine restrictions and replace them with proportionate, as-needed measures wherever possible.

5→1

Routine kitchen restrictions reduced to one PRN measure

Instead of locking cupboards, removing objects and restricting the fridge as routine, one enclosed kitchen restriction could be used only when genuinely required.

The starting point

The organisation originally explored Maybo because physical restraint was written into the participant’s support arrangements and staff needed appropriate training.

The shift in thinking

Training reframed the task: not “how do we restrain safely?” but “what can we understand, change or prevent so restraint is not needed?”

The home environment

Routine restrictions meant the participant could not freely access the kitchen, develop cooking skills or enjoy ordinary activities such as baking.

A more proportionate plan

At baseline, the kitchen remained accessible. During periods of serious aggression, the door could be locked temporarily and the duration recorded.

The wider result

Greater freedom, more meaningful life skills and fewer restrictions—supported by staff who understood the reasons behind behaviour and could document change.

“The idea is to give freedom back to our participants—not to continue stopping them from accessing the community, their own house or food.”
David Brimfield · Unique Support Services
What changed for staff

Confidence became a system, not a feeling.

Shared training gave teams a common language for decisions, reporting, handovers, debriefs and support after difficult incidents.

01

Better dynamic decisions

Staff became more able to assess risk on the fly, create space, remove hazards and choose less restrictive responses.

02

Stronger teamwork

Colleagues could switch the lead support role, discuss options using the same language and avoid leaving one person to carry the full burden.

03

More useful reporting

An initial rise in reports reflected better recognition and documentation, often capturing lower-severity events that had previously been missed.

04

Evidence-led plan reviews

Repeated evidence that a strategy was not working gave practitioners a sound basis to revise behaviour support plans.

05

Post-incident care

Every report should prompt a debrief, validation and access to support—not silence followed by uncertainty.

06

Long-term relationships

Supporting staff after incidents helps retain experienced people who can continue building trust with participants.

Turning incidents into learning

Three questions changed the quality of the evidence.

Reports moved beyond “it came out of nowhere”. Staff began identifying setting events and longer build-ups: poor sleep, an upsetting event at school, a broken phone, embarrassment or stress from earlier in the week.

David’s message to other organisations

Invest in the values behind the training.

The greatest value does not come from physically engaging with a person. It comes from gathering and updating information, building confidence from the ground up and helping staff form a working alliance with the individual.

That understanding creates the conditions to challenge restrictions accumulated over a lifetime—and to improve quality of life in practical, lasting ways.

Relationship

Understanding

Evidence
